fieldsRead.text: Dutch, European and International Law, formerly European Law School, combines Dutch law with European Union and international law. This comparison follows the regular full-time pathway in the current regulations.

The UCR programme combines substantive constitutional, criminal, private, EU, human-rights, international and transnational business law with cross-border governance, politics and social inquiry. Legal research, advice and simulated arbitration provide practical contributions. It does not reproduce Radboud’s full Dutch civil and procedural sequence, specialist research requirements, criminal/EU moot courts or compulsory legal thesis.

Each year contains 60 EC. The programme requires 176 EC of compulsory study plus one 4-EC restricted metajuridical choice, shown here as Philosophy of Law. There is no open elective space. Noncredit first-year Tutoraat participation and active, prepared participation are additional requirements. The ordinary first-year study-advice threshold is 45 EC. Later-year study requires completion of the first year, or at least 45 EC plus the relevant subject prerequisites. Completing the full first year satisfies that general entry condition.

Required 5-EC legal thesis, 4000–5000 words. Entry requires Academic Language Skills and Academic Skills I and II; mandatory group meetings apply. Topic-specific course requirements may also apply when published for the selected topic.
Choose one 4-EC metajuridical subject: European legal history, sociology of law or philosophy of law. This example selects philosophy of law.

Both develop academic writing, source evaluation and research communication. UCR also includes civic and reflective formation and does not reproduce the full law-specific skills curriculum.
Both introduce the main legal fields, while UCR also treats social and normative approaches and does not replicate the full Dutch legal sequence.

Both study constitutional institutions and rights comparatively. UCR compares several jurisdictions and includes administrative-law principles; it does not reproduce the sustained Dutch and comparative constitutional-law requirement.
Both teach criminal liability and principles of criminal justice; the external curriculum develops Dutch procedure more extensively.
Both examine private-law relationships and obligations; UCR introduces principles rather than a multi-year civil-law sequence.

Both introduce the EU legal order, its institutions, sources and relationship to member-state law. UCR also applies judicial-remedy and free-movement rules; it is one course rather than the full specialist EU sequence.
Both study human-rights legal instruments and institutions; UCR also adds philosophical and historical analysis.

Both develop written legal argument and oral advocacy in a simulated dispute. UCR uses international commercial arbitration, while Radboud requires an international/EU-law moot court; jurisdiction, procedure and subject coverage differ.
Both introduce the sources and actors of public international law.

Radboud requires a sustained Dutch civil and procedural sequence, specialist legal research, subject-specific moot courts and a 5-EC legal thesis. This UCR programme provides substantive law, legal case analysis, comparative research and simulated arbitration alongside political and social study. These are meaningful contributions, while the full Dutch requirements and professional legal qualification remain distinct.

selectedDescriptionsRead.ACCPPDE101: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
selectedDescriptionsRead.BENBUSI311: Transnational Business Law studies legal frameworks for cross-border business, including contracts, trade, intellectual property, foreign investment and digital commerce. Comparative and international perspectives support analysis of legal risks through discussions, problem-based assignments and an arbitration simulation.
selectedDescriptionsRead.BENGATE101: Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation. The class fosters creativity and collaboration to drive business and social innovation.
selectedDescriptionsRead.ENSDELT312: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSGATE102: Law, Society & Justice examines legal, social and normative perspectives on law. Students compare legal traditions and study public and private law, human rights, justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, demand letters and mock trials develop legal reasoning, while a family-law topic supports the design of a socio-legal research proposal.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSHIST112: Studies gender, storytelling and marginalised lives in the nineteenth- to twenty-first-century American context. Students examine slavery, community activism, representation and lived experience, using sources and projects that connect historical interpretation with contemporary questions.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSLAWJ111: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSLAWJ211: Examines moral and legal justifications for criminalisation and punishment. Investigates guiding principles of criminal law and justice, including criminal accountability, guilt, legality and fundamental principles, and applies theory through a simulated legal aid clinic.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSLAWJ212: Introduction to Public International Law examines its sources, theories, institutions and relationship to domestic law. Topics include responsibility, force, armed conflict, international crime, human rights, economic relations and environmental protection, followed by self-determination, Third World approaches, compliance and treaty politics. Case exercises and a research podcast develop legal reasoning and critical analysis.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSLAWJ213: Comparative Constitutional Law compares constitutional structures, institutions and rights across legal systems and introduces administrative law. Students study federalism, legislatures, executive relationships, courts, judicial review, human rights, public participation and procedural fairness. A staged booklet compares two constitutions, supported by legal interpretation, case-law analysis and hypothetical cases.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSLAWJ311: Examines principles of property, tort and contract law and other selected areas of private law. It compares legal systems including Germany, France, England, China and the United States, and considers the social, economic and political pressures underlying legal principles.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSLAWJ312: Introduces the EU legal order. Studies institutions, framework, citizenship and the internal market using problem‑based exercises and guest lectures.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSPHIL212: Ethics examines moral reasoning through historical and contemporary theories and close philosophical reading. Students study utilitarianism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics, alongside Nietzsche, Murdoch and Nagel. Reflection and research essays develop interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSPOLI112: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSPOLI212: Theory of International Relations introduces competing approaches to international relations and geopolitics, including realism, liberalism, Marxism, constructivism and critical theory. Students apply theories to historical and contemporary cases. A United Nations Security Council simulation develops country-position research, negotiation and collaborative resolution drafting.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSPOLI311: European Union Politics examines EU institutions, actors, integration and policymaking, including representation, legitimacy and decision-making. An empirical project investigates European Parliament committee amendments, relating MEP ideology and possible interest-group influence to amendment activity. Students plan the research, code amendments, assess salience and trace legislative processes.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSPOLI313: Peace & Conflict examines conflict and approaches to peace through legal, sociological, political and historical perspectives. Structural inequality, identity and colonial legacies connect to international security, humanitarian law, human rights, peacebuilding and transitional justice. An interdisciplinary podcast, policy brief and research dossier develop analysis, while reflection examines how assumptions shape inquiry.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSSOCI111: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSSOCI212: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSSOCI215: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSSOCI311: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory studies civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial perspectives. Topics include trust, social capital, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair. An experience report connects engagement or observation to course concepts, while an individual project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyse a civil-society organisation, movement or initiative.
selectedDescriptionsRead.MCCCOMM111: The Art of Rhetorical Communication develops rhetorical analysis, academic writing and oral presentation. Students examine classical Western roots and the canons of rhetoric, and learn to construct, organise and support persuasive arguments. Historical and contemporary examples connect rhetorical theory with practical communication.
selectedDescriptionsRead.BENENTR312: This course examines the institutional, political and cultural forces shaping global businesses. It first explores how international companies operate, then centers on key global challenges including cross-border governance, corporate responsibility, geopolitical strategies and global trade. It provides a comprehensive understanding of today’s complex international business environment.
selectedDescriptionsRead.MCCCOMM311: Persuasive Communication studies persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis. Students examine framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Community-engaged projects develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles, while an individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools.
